newsitem.title: USA: First Union acquisition of Signet seen expensive.
newsitem.headline: First Union acquisition of Signet seen expensive.

text.p: First Union Corp's planned $3.25 billion acquisition of Signet Banking Corp is an expensive deal but has a good chance of paying off, given First Union's track record, analysts said Monday.
"I think we've reached a mind-numbing new pleateau for pricing deals," said Nancy Bush, analyst at Brown Brothers Harriman.
She noted First Union is paying about 23 times the 1997 consensus earnings estimate for Signet of $2.34 a share. The consensus estimate for 1998 is about $2.82 a share, she said.
The companies said Signet shareholders will receive 0.55 share of First Union for each share of Signet.
With a two-for-one split in the stock of First Union previously announced and payable July 31, the exchange ratio would be 1.10 shares.
Based on First Union's closing stock price of $97.44 on Friday, Signet holders would receive First Union stock worth $53.59 for each of their shares. Signet closed at 36-11/16 Friday.
"There is no question that the price is expensive," said Moshe Orenbuch, analyst at Sanford C. Bernstein Co. He said First Union is paying about 3.4 times book value.
But he added, "The reality is that they can make the numbers work."
First Union said the merger, which is expected to close by year-end, will have a positive effect on earnings in 1998 and will be increasingly positive thereafter.
"Our read is that First Union's earnings for 1998 will be higher with Signet than without," said Anthony Davis, analyst at Dillon Read & Co Inc.
While the recission of First Union's stock buyback program, which is required under pooling-of-interest merger rules, will be a negative for earnings, Davis expects this to be offset by cost savings.
He also said he expects a resumption of share repurchases at the end of July 1998.
On balance, Davis expects First Union earnings of about $8.05 per share in 1998, compared to his previous estimate of $8.00
First Union said it expects to save 50 percent of Signet's annual expenses, or $242 million.
"First Union has gotten credibility for the deals it has done over the last two or three years," said Orenbuch.

In the biggest deal in that period -- the acquisition of New Jersey-based First Fidelity Bancorp -- "they have done better than plan on costs and a lot better on revenue, which I think was the big surprise," he said.

Thomas McCandless, analyst at NatWest Markets, said he was surprised at the timing of the Signet deal, which came less than two months after Signet announced a "redesign" of its business. But he also said he was pleased because Signet was his most aggressive buy recommendation.

He said the redesign has involved pruning branches in less populous areas. He said Signet has made its mark with national direct marketing of banking products, and national marketing is likely to be enhanced as a result of the First Union deal. "They (First Union) have deeper pockets and I'm sure First Union is committed to that," McCandless said.

"Signet has begun to carve out a strategy centered around alternative delivery of retail product," Bush said. "First Union has touted that, so there should be a meeting of the minds in the strategic sense."

Bush also said the deal looked "defensive" for First Union because one of its competitors in North Carolina, Wachovia Corp, recently agreed to buy Central Fidelity Banks Inc and Jefferson Bankshares, both headquartered in Virgina.

The First Union and Wachovia deals turned the spotlight on Virgina's biggest independent bank, Crestar Financial Corp. "Crestar has clearly got more eyes looking at it today than they did Friday,' Davis said.
Signet shares were up 13-6/16 at 50-1/16 in late-morning trade. First Union was off 3-1/4 at 94-3/16.
